Expected Information Gain is a Bet Against Uninformative Data

Published on 2026-10-26.

#bayesian-experimental-design

The expected information gain (EIG, Lindley, 1956), the expected reduction in Shannon (or differential) entropy from the prior to the posterior, is a popular objective in Bayesian experimental design. It has several useful interpretations: it is the mutual information between the data and the latent parameters of interest zzz, and it is the expected reduction in Bayes risk for a decision problem under the logarithmic score (see my earlier post on expected information as expected utility). This post is about yet another interpretation: the EIG is the optimal growth rate of a bettor who bets against the null hypothesis that the data are uninformative about zzz.

I begin by reviewing Kelly’s result on betting with side information and its connection to the more general testing-by-betting paradigm, and then show that the EIG is exactly Kelly’s growth rate when the side information is zzz.

A Brief Review of Kelly Betting

Kelly (1956) considered a gambler with access to side information. Suppose that in each round a pair (Yi,Zi)(Y_{i}, Z_{i})(Yi​,Zi​) is drawn i.i.d. from a joint distribution q(y,z)q(y, z)q(y,z), with YiY_{i}Yi​ taking values in a finite set Y\mathcal{Y}Y. The bookmaker knows only the marginal law q(y)q(y)q(y) of the outcome and offers fair odds accordingly: a unit stake on outcome yyy returns 1/q(y)1/q(y)1/q(y) if Yi=yY_{i} = yYi​=y and nothing otherwise. We, however, receive ZiZ_{i}Zi​ over a “private wire” before each round. We start with an initial wealth V0V_{0}V0​, and in each round we observe Zi=zZ_{i} = zZi​=z and stake a fraction b(y∣z)b(y \mid z)b(y∣z) of our current wealth on each y∈Yy \in \mathcal{Y}y∈Y. Kelly asked which strategy bbb maximises the logarithmic rate of growth1 of our wealth, G(b)=lim⁡N→∞1Nlog⁡VNV0,G(b) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N} \log \frac{V_{N}}{V_{0}},G(b)=N→∞lim​N1​logV0​VN​​, where VNV_{N}VN​ is our wealth after round NNN. Throughout, log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm; Kelly used base 2, which only changes the units from nats to bits. By the law of large numbers, with probability one we have G(b)=E[log⁡b(Y∣Z)q(Y)]=Eq(z)[KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]−KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ b(⋅∣z)]].G(b) = \mathbb{E}\left[\log \frac{b(Y \mid Z)}{q(Y)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\Big[\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q] - \operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, b(\cdot \mid z)]\Big].G(b)=E[logq(Y)b(Y∣Z)​]=Eq(z)​[KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q]−KL[q(⋅∣z)∥b(⋅∣z)]]. Since the KL divergence is non-negative and zero only when its arguments coincide, Kelly’s result follows immediately: the optimal strategy and the resulting optimal rate of growth are b⋆(y∣z)=q(y∣z),G(b⋆)=Eq(z)[KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]]=I(Y;Z).b^{\star}(y \mid z) = q(y \mid z), \qquad G(b^{\star}) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\left[\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]\right] = I(Y; Z).b⋆(y∣z)=q(y∣z),G(b⋆)=Eq(z)​[KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q]]=I(Y;Z). Here I(Y;Z)I(Y; Z)I(Y;Z) is the mutual information between YYY and ZZZ, defined by the middle expression: the average KL divergence of the conditional law of YYY given ZZZ from its marginal law, or equivalently KL⁡[q(y,z) ∥ q(y) q(z)]\operatorname{KL}[q(y, z) \,\Vert\, q(y) \, q(z)]KL[q(y,z)∥q(y)q(z)]. In words, we should bet on each outcome in proportion to our belief in it given what the wire tells us, and our wealth then grows at a rate equal to the mutual information between the wire and the outcome. If the wire carries no information (ZZZ independent of YYY), the best we can do is break even.

Testing by Betting

Kelly’s formulation extends naturally to statistical testing, an idea known as testing by betting (Shafer, 2021; Shafer and Vovk, 2019). To see how, suppose the wire always carries the same message zzz, so that the outcomes are i.i.d. draws from q(⋅∣z)q(\cdot \mid z)q(⋅∣z), while the bookmaker still prices them at qqq. Betting against this bookmaker is then a test of the null hypothesis H0 ⁣:Yi∼qH_{0}\colon Y_{i} \sim qH0​:Yi​∼q against the alternative H1 ⁣:Yi∼q(⋅∣z)H_{1}\colon Y_{i} \sim q(\cdot \mid z)H1​:Yi​∼q(⋅∣z): the bookmaker believes the null, and we measure the evidence against it by how much money we make.

If we follow Kelly’s strategy and bet b⋆(⋅∣z)=q(⋅∣z)b^{\star}(\cdot \mid z) = q(\cdot \mid z)b⋆(⋅∣z)=q(⋅∣z), then in round sss our wealth is multiplied by Es=q(ys∣z)q(ys),E_{s} = \frac{q(y_{s} \mid z)}{q(y_{s})},Es​=q(ys​)q(ys​∣z)​, so starting from V0=1V_{0} = 1V0​=1, our wealth after ttt rounds is Mt=∏s=1tEs=∏s=1tq(ys∣z)q(ys),M_{t} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} E_{s} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{q(y_{s} \mid z)}{q(y_{s})},Mt​=s=1∏t​Es​=s=1∏t​q(ys​)q(ys​∣z)​, which is simply the likelihood ratio of the data. Since the odds are fair under the null, we cannot expect to make money if the null is true: Eq[Es]=1andEq[Mt+1∣Y1:t]=Mt.\mathbb{E}_{q}[E_{s}] = 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbb{E}_{q}[M_{t+1} \mid Y_{1:t}] = M_{t}.Eq​[Es​]=1andEq​[Mt+1​∣Y1:t​]=Mt​. That is, MtM_{t}Mt​ is a non-negative martingale under H0H_{0}H0​ with M0=1M_{0} = 1M0​=1, known as a test martingale. By Ville’s inequality, for any α∈(0,1)\alpha \in (0, 1)α∈(0,1), Pq(∃ t ⁣:Mt≥1/α)≤α,\mathbb{P}_{q}\left(\exists\, t \colon M_{t} \geq 1/\alpha\right) \leq \alpha,Pq​(∃t:Mt​≥1/α)≤α, so rejecting H0H_{0}H0​ as soon as our wealth reaches 1/α1/\alpha1/α is a level-α\alphaα test.

Each EsE_{s}Es​ is an e-variable, a non-negative statistic with expectation at most 111 under the null, and MtM_{t}Mt​ is an e-process, a non-negative process satisfying Eq[Mτ]≤1\mathbb{E}_{q}[M_{\tau}] \leq 1Eq​[Mτ​]≤1 for every stopping time τ\tauτ (Ramdas and Wang, 2025). Kelly’s theorem tells us which bet to make when the alternative is true. If Yi∼q(⋅∣z)Y_{i} \sim q(\cdot \mid z)Yi​∼q(⋅∣z), then 1tlog⁡Mt→KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]\frac{1}{t} \log M_{t} \to \operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]t1​logMt​→KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q] almost surely, so our wealth grows exponentially and we eventually reject the null. Moreover, no other e-variable for this null grows faster. Grünwald et al. (2024) call this the growth-rate optimal (GRO) criterion. For a simple null and a simple alternative, the GRO e-variable is exactly the likelihood ratio q(⋅∣z)/qq(\cdot \mid z)/qq(⋅∣z)/q, and its growth rate is KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q], the term inside the expectation in Kelly’s growth rate.

The Experimental Design Setting

Let zzz be a latent variable with prior p(z)p(z)p(z). At each step t∈{1,…,T}t \in \{1, \dots, T\}t∈{1,…,T}, the experimenter chooses a design xtx_{t}xt​ according to a policy, xt∼π(⋅∣ht−1)x_{t} \sim \pi(\cdot \mid h_{t-1})xt​∼π(⋅∣ht−1​), and observes an outcome yt∼p(⋅∣z,xt,ht−1)y_{t} \sim p(\cdot \mid z, x_{t}, h_{t-1})yt​∼p(⋅∣z,xt​,ht−1​), where ht=((x1,y1),…,(xt,yt))h_{t} = ((x_{1}, y_{1}), \dots, (x_{t}, y_{t}))ht​=((x1​,y1​),…,(xt​,yt​)) is the history so far and h0=∅h_{0} = \emptyseth0​=∅. Since the policy depends only on the history and not on zzz, its terms cancel in Bayes’ rule, and the posterior is p(z∣ht)∝p(z)∏s=1tp(ys∣z,xs,hs−1).p(z \mid h_{t}) \propto p(z) \prod_{s=1}^{t} p(y_{s} \mid z, x_{s}, h_{s-1}).p(z∣ht​)∝p(z)s=1∏t​p(ys​∣z,xs​,hs−1​). This ratio has an interpretation as the wealth process of an oracle who knows the true parameter zzz. To see this, we apply Bayes’ rule repeatedly and factorise the above ratio as Et(z)=∏s=1tp(ys∣z,xs,hs−1)p(ys∣xs,hs−1).(2)E_{t}(z) = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{p(y_{s} \mid z, x_{s}, h_{s-1})}{p(y_{s} \mid x_{s}, h_{s-1})}. \tag{2}Et​(z)=s=1∏t​p(ys​∣xs​,hs−1​)p(ys​∣z,xs​,hs−1​)​.(2) Each factor in the above equation has a betting interpretation. Her wealth is then multiplied by the sss-th factor in (2), so Et(z)E_{t}(z)Et​(z) is her wealth after ttt design steps, whichever policy chose the designs.

The Uninformative Null and the EIG

We can now treat one entire experiment as a single round of Kelly’s game. Nature draws z∼p(z)z \sim p(z)z∼p(z), which the oracle receives over the private wire, and the outcome she bets on is the whole history hTh_{T}hT​. The bookmaker, who does not know zzz, prices this outcome at its marginal law p(hT)p(h_{T})p(hT​) under the policy π\piπ; equivalently, by (2), the bookmaker quotes the posterior predictive odds one design step at a time, and the oracle places her bet one step at a time too.

Fix zzz. The natural null hypothesis is that the experiment is uninformative, that is, the data carry no trace of zzz: H0 ⁣:hT∼p(hT)H_{0}\colon h_{T} \sim p(h_{T})H0​:hT​∼p(hT​), against the alternative H1 ⁣:hT∼p(hT∣z)H_{1}\colon h_{T} \sim p(h_{T} \mid z)H1​:hT​∼p(hT​∣z). As before, the policy’s terms cancel in the likelihood ratio, p(hT∣z)p(hT)=p(z∣hT)p(z)=ET(z),(3)\frac{p(h_{T} \mid z)}{p(h_{T})} = \frac{p(z \mid h_{T})}{p(z)} = E_{T}(z), \tag{3}p(hT​)p(hT​∣z)​=p(z)p(z∣hT​)​=ET​(z),(3) so the oracle’s wealth is exactly the likelihood ratio of the alternative against the null, just as MtM_{t}Mt​ was in the testing-by-betting section, and hence the GRO e-variable for this test. It is straightforward to show that, under the null, (Et(z))0≤t≤T(E_{t}(z))_{0 \leq t \leq T}(Et​(z))0≤t≤T​ is a non-negative martingale with E0(z)=1E_{0}(z) = 1E0​(z)=1, so the oracle’s wealth is a test martingale for every zzz. In betting terms, the bookmaker’s odds are fair under the null, so even the oracle cannot expect to make money if zzz leaves no trace in the data. The optimal growth rate of the test is KL⁡[p(hT∣z) ∥ p(hT)]\operatorname{KL}[p(h_{T} \mid z) \,\Vert\, p(h_{T})]KL[p(hT​∣z)∥p(hT​)].

Averaging over the message on the wire, Kelly’s theorem gives the oracle’s growth rate across repeated experiments as Ep(z)[KL⁡[p(hT∣z) ∥ p(hT)]]=I(z;hT)=EIG⁡T(π).(4)\mathbb{E}_{p(z)}\left[\operatorname{KL}[p(h_{T} \mid z) \,\Vert\, p(h_{T})]\right] = I(z; h_{T}) = \operatorname{EIG}_{T}(\pi). \tag{4}Ep(z)​[KL[p(hT​∣z)∥p(hT​)]]=I(z;hT​)=EIGT​(π).(4) That is, the EIG is exactly Kelly’s growth rate for a gambler whose private wire carries zzz, betting on the outcome of the experiment against a bookmaker who believes it is uninformative about zzz.

Conclusion

Seen this way, experimental design is the problem of choosing which game to play. The bookmaker always offers fair odds under the model, so no experiment lets a bettor without knowledge of zzz make money. What the policy π\piπ controls is how much the private wire is worth: an informative experiment is one in which knowing zzz lets the oracle beat the bookmaker quickly, and the EIG-optimal policy is the one that makes this edge as large as possible. In testing terms, maximising the EIG chooses the experiment that, on average over the prior, gathers evidence fastest against the hypothesis that we learn nothing about zzz.
